text: Advertisement Tedious. Mind-numbing. Soul-destroying. Ask visual-effects artists in Hollywood and most will agree: The task known as rotoscoping, while essential, is no fun. Perhaps that is why an industry that has at times had its pitchforks out for everything artificial intelligence seems open to the idea that the technology can alleviate this particular burden. Rotoscoping — even the name is insipid — involves methodically tracing around an object or a person, frame by frame and often for hours so that it can be isolated from the rest of the shot. A hologram of Princess Leia does not plead for help from Obi-Wan Kenobi in the original “Star Wars” (1977) without rotoscoping. Nor do the light sabers glow. But can A.I. ease the drudgery? And can it do so with the same expert precision that human hands have provided for decades? What happens to those workers if their jobs get replaced? More than a dozen people who work in visual effects in Hollywood acknowledged in interviews that some of the A.I.-powered rotoscoping tools they have begun to tinker with may be saving time and reducing tedium. But they stressed that the tools were far from perfect. Almost more important, they added, rotoscoping is a slice of moviemaking that offers valuable insight into how A.I. has begun to influence the industry. “A.I. is not a simple conversation,” said Sang-Jin Bae, the director of the Martin Scorsese Virtual Production Center at New York University. But rotoscoping, he added, “is actually the perfect case study.” Thank you for your patience while we verify access.
